## A small page, a new skill

This Quarto report explores how a local document becomes a webpage. It brings together structured content, CSS styling, and a plan for publishing with GitHub Pages.

[Visit my About Me page](about.html){.btn .btn-primary}

## How the pieces fit together

| Tool | Purpose |
|:--|:--|
| Quarto | Render a report into an HTML document |
| HTML | Give the page headings, paragraphs, links, and lists |
| CSS | Control color, spacing, typography, and layout |
| GitHub Pages | Publish repository files as a website |

## HTML example

The About Me page uses semantic HTML. A heading introduces the page and a paragraph provides context.

```html
<section id="about">
  <h2>About me</h2>
  <p>I am exploring how to build and publish a webpage.</p>
</section>
```

## CSS example

This rule gives the page its dark blue text and light background. CSS classes let several elements share the same style.

```css
body {
  color: #172b4d;
  background: #f3f6fc;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
}
```

## Publishing plan

1. Create a GitHub repository.
2. Upload `index.html`, `about.html`, and `styles.css` to the root of `main`.
3. In **Settings → Pages**, select **Deploy from a branch**, **main**, and **/(root)**.
4. Open the URL that GitHub provides once deployment finishes.

The default filename `index.html` lets the server find a site's home page without requiring a filename in the URL.

## Reflection

HTML describes the meaning and structure of content. CSS controls its presentation. Rendering a document creates a local file; publishing makes that file accessible through a web address.
